channel.title: The Talk Therapy Podcast
channel.description:
Welcome to Talk Therapy, the podcast about the small shifts that make a big difference. I’m your host, Sarah Miller, and today we’re talking about incomplete things. Not big projects, not life goals – the little stuff. The things we *start* with good intentions, but then… just leave. That half-finished mug. That email drafted but unsent. That book begun but abandoned. We’ll explore why we do that, and what it might be okay to let go of.
--- Transcript ---
TITLE: The Half-Finished Mug
(Sound of someone sighing, then a gentle clink of a mug being set down) Ever notice how many half-finished mugs of tea or coffee you have around? It’s… a little telling, isn’t it?
Welcome to Talk Therapy, the podcast about the small shifts that make a big difference. I’m your host, Sarah Miller, and today we’re talking about incomplete things. Not big projects, not life goals – the little stuff. The things we *start* with good intentions, but then… just leave. That half-finished mug. That email drafted but unsent. That book begun but abandoned. We’ll explore why we do that, and what it might be okay to let go of.
I was talking to a friend, Liam, last week. He’s a really creative guy, always starting new hobbies. He’d recently taken up watercolor painting, bought all the supplies, watched a ton of tutorials… and then stopped after one painting. He felt *guilty* about it. He’d spent money, he’d been excited, and now it was just… sitting there. He said he felt like a failure, like he lacked discipline. But as we talked, it wasn't about the painting at all. It was about the pressure he put on himself to be *good* immediately. He hadn’t allowed himself to simply enjoy the process of learning something new. He’d skipped right to judging the outcome. And that one unfinished painting became a symbol of all the things he felt he wasn't "good enough" to continue.
Liam’s experience really resonated with me because I think we all do this, on some level. We get caught in this cycle of initiation and then… stall. And often, it’s not about the task itself being difficult or unpleasant. It’s about what that task *represents*. Sometimes it represents a fear of not being perfect. Sometimes it's a fear of investing time and energy into something that might not “work out.” And sometimes, honestly, it's just a sign that our initial enthusiasm wasn’t really aligned with our actual priorities.
There's a concept in psychology called “goal gradient effect.” Basically, as you get closer to a goal, your motivation *increases*. But the opposite is also true – the further away you feel from a goal, the less motivated you become. Starting something gives you that initial burst of motivation, but if it quickly feels overwhelming or distant, that motivation can plummet. This isn’t a character flaw; it's just how our brains work.
Another thing to consider is the value we place on completion. Our culture often equates finishing something with success. But what if success isn't always about finishing? What if success is about exploring, learning, and being willing to change course? Maybe Liam didn’t need to become a watercolor artist. Maybe he needed to discover that he enjoys other creative outlets more.
So, what can we do with all these half-finished things? I want you to think of one small, incomplete task in your life right now. Something that's been lingering and causing you a little bit of low-level stress. It could be anything – a book, a craft project, a letter you meant to write.
Now, instead of trying to *finish* it, I want you to give yourself permission to *release* it. Literally. If it's a physical object, can you donate it? Repurpose it? Give it away? If it's something digital, can you delete the draft? If it’s an idea, can you simply acknowledge that it’s okay to let it go?
As you release it, say to yourself – silently or out loud – "This doesn't need to be finished for me to be okay." Or "I'm choosing to free up energy for things that feel more aligned with me now." The point isn't to beat yourself up about not finishing; it's to practice letting go of things that no longer serve you. It's about reclaiming your energy and your attention. It’s about recognizing that starting something isn't failure; abandoning something that isn’t right for you isn't failure either.
That’s all for today’s episode of Talk Therapy. Remember, it’s okay to have half-finished mugs – and half-finished projects – in your life. It’s part of being human. Be kind to yourself, and tune in next week for more small shifts towards a more grounded you.

item.title: The Talk Therapy — (Sound of a deflating balloon)
item.description:
Welcome to Talk Therapy, the podcast about the everyday moments that shape our inner lives. I’m your host, Sarah Miller, and I’m a facilitator of conversations, not a giver of advice. We explore the little things, the human experiences we all share, and hopefully, find a little more understanding along the way. This week, we're digging into the surprisingly powerful emotions that surface when we experience “almost” – almost getting the job, almost finishing a project, almost saying what we meant
--- Transcript ---
TITLE: The Weight of Almost
(Sound of a deflating balloon) Ever feel like you’re *so* close to something, and then… it slips away? That feeling of almost? Today, we’re talking about navigating that space.
Welcome to Talk Therapy, the podcast about the everyday moments that shape our inner lives. I’m your host, Sarah Miller, and I’m a facilitator of conversations, not a giver of advice. We explore the little things, the human experiences we all share, and hopefully, find a little more understanding along the way. This week, we're digging into the surprisingly powerful emotions that surface when we experience “almost” – almost getting the job, almost finishing a project, almost saying what we meant to say. It’s a tricky space, full of potential and frustration.
I was talking to a friend, Liam, last week. He'd been working towards a promotion at work for almost a year. He put in extra hours, took on challenging projects, really went above and beyond. He was *certain* he was going to get it. He even started mentally redecorating his new office! Then, they announced the promotion went to someone else. It wasn't about Liam’s performance, apparently; the other candidate had a very specific skillset for a new initiative. But Liam was… gutted. Not just disappointed, but deeply, surprisingly affected. He kept saying, “I was *right there*.” It wasn’t the lack of the promotion itself, it was the sting of being so close. That feeling of almost is a very particular kind of pain.
And that pain makes sense. We tend to focus on the outcome – the promotion, the finished painting, the perfect sentence. But our brains are also wired to notice the *gap* between our effort and the result. That gap is where "almost" lives. And it triggers something primal in us. Historically, being “almost” successful at hunting or gathering could still mean going hungry. That sense of needing to close the gap for survival is still present today, even if the stakes aren’t life or death.
Another thing to consider is that “almost” often highlights what we value. Liam wasn't upset because he didn't want *any* promotion; he was upset because he wanted *this* one. It revealed how much he valued recognition for his hard work and the opportunity to lead that new initiative. The discomfort is actually information – it tells us what’s important to us.
Finally, and this is important: “almost” isn’t failure. It’s not even necessarily a setback. It's simply a data point. It tells us where we are in relation to where we want to be. It's information that can inform our next steps, but it doesn’t define our worth or our capabilities. We often treat “almost” as though it's a lesser version of success, but it’s a unique experience with its own lessons.
So how do we navigate this tricky emotional terrain? Let’s try a small exercise I suggested to Liam. It's called "The Almost Reflection." Grab a journal or a piece of paper. And I mean now – pause the podcast if you need to! Okay, got your paper?
Think of a recent "almost" experience – something you were really hoping for that didn't quite materialize. Write down three things: First, what exactly did you want? Be specific. Second, what did you learn from the experience? Not about what you *should* have done differently, but what did you learn about yourself? What values were highlighted? And finally, what’s one small, concrete step you can take *now* that feels aligned with those values? It doesn't have to be related to the original “almost” situation. Maybe it’s signing up for a class, reaching out to a friend, or simply taking 15 minutes for yourself today.
The goal isn't to erase the disappointment; it’s to acknowledge it, extract the learning, and move forward with intention. The “Almost Reflection” is about shifting your focus from what didn't happen to what you *can* do. It's about reclaiming your agency in the face of uncertainty.
Remember, feeling the weight of “almost” is human. It means you care, you strive, and you're engaged with life. Be kind to yourself when those feelings arise. And until next time, thank you for listening to Talk Therapy.
